title: Russia’s Kaliningrad threats show the value of Baltic preparedness
gist: Chatham House argues Baltic states' defence spending, border fortification and whole-of-society resilience have made the NATO Baltic flank harder to overrun, even as Putin's Kaliningrad nuclear rhetoric must be taken seriously.

insights.claim: On 1 October Putin said a direct attack on Kaliningrad would put all weapons in Russia's arsenal on the table, following a Russian note to NATO threatening nuclear escalation if the alliance isolated the enclave.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Raises tail risk premium for Baltic and European security.

insights.claim: Russia's 2024 nuclear doctrine revision explicitly broadened circumstances for nuclear use to include threats to territorial integrity and attempts to isolate parts of Russian territory.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Makes isolation of Kaliningrad a stated nuclear trigger.

insights.claim: Lithuania may soon vote to lift its ban on hosting nuclear weapons, which the Kremlin called a step towards escalating tensions.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Watch Lithuanian vote for escalation signals.

insights.claim: The Baltic states have little strategic depth and rely on the 65km Suwałki corridor for reinforcement, so their strategy is to stop Russian advance from the first battles at the border.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Defence demand for fortifications, anti-tank and air defence in the region.
insights.quote: We have to start from the border and win from the first battles

insights.claim: A permanent German armoured brigade becomes operational in Lithuania in 2027, and Estonia's defence spending is nearly 5.5% of GDP.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Signals sustained European defence spending far above the old 2% target.

insights.claim: Baltic air and missile defence remains thin relative to Russia's drone and missile arsenal, leaving the states reliant on allied reinforcements.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Air and missile defence is the clear capability gap.

insights.claim: Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania have disconnected their electricity systems from Russian and Belarusian networks, progressively synchronizing with the continental grid since February 2025.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Grid decoupling reduces energy leverage and sabotage exposure.

insights.claim: Germany's shelter capacity covers only about 480,000 people and it approved a €10bn civil-defence programme to convert car parks, tunnels and stations into shelters.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Civil-defence capex is a growing European spending category.

insights.claim: NATO's new resilience baseline requirements ask governments to plan for population movements, mass-casualty-capable health systems and transport and communications that support allied forces in high-intensity conflict.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Resilience requirements will drive infrastructure and healthcare spending.

insights.claim: Baltic resilience changes Moscow's calculation by making any attack look slower and costlier, and strategic weight is not measured by size alone.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Deterrence-by-resilience lowers the probability of a quick-win Russian incursion.
